newsitem.title: JAPAN: Forex unlikely to be main topic at G7 talks - Kubo.
newsitem.headline: Forex unlikely to be main topic at G7 talks - Kubo.

text.p: The issue of currencies is unlikely to be discussed at length should the finance ministers and central bank governors of the Group of Seven (G7) nations meet in Washington later this week, Japanese Finance Minister Wataru Kubo told a news conference on Tuesday.
G7 finance ministers and central bank governors are widely expected to meet later this week in Washington on the sidelines of the semi-annual meeting of the IMF and World Bank as they usually do.

Asked whether currencies would be a main topic at such a G7 meeting, Kubo told a regular news conference: "I don't think the issue of currencies would be a theme which the nations would spend much time discussing... There is no change in our view that currencies have been moving in a welcome direction as the result of coordination and cooperation between the G7 to seek currency stability since April last year."
Kubo added that at the IMF meeting, the major nations might instead focus on the issues of debt relief for their debtor nations and proposed sales of gold held by the IMF.

Asked whether Japan is likely to be pressed by other nations to add more fiscal spending to help its economy, Kubo said that the government was aware of various requests from other nations, including the United States. He did not elaborate.

"We should always make much of any requests and opinions from other nations about Japan's economic stimulative measures in an era of globalisation. However, we must make our own judgement on whether to take fiscal steps for the economy, taking into consideration our own fiscal situation."
"Judging from indicators showing economic trends up to now, I believe we still need to be cautious about drafting a large-scale supplementary budget as a way to stimulate the economy," Kubo said.
He said Japan's tax system is unlikely to be a topic for discussion by the G7.

Kubo said he was not in a position to say whether there would be a change in a planned rise in Japan's consumption tax, which is due to take place in April next year. The tax rate is due to be raised to five percent from the current three percent.
He added, however, that parliament and the government needed to discuss possible improvements or revisions of the current system for the consumption tax.
Asked whether there would be any revision in the tax system before April 1997, Kubo said he was not in a position to say whether such a revision was possible.

Japanese media have reported that some lawmakers in the three-party ruling coalition are considering proposing a smaller increase in the consumption tax on food in an attempt to win votes in a Lower House election expected to take place next month.
